nameStory: Branch Bumps gets its name from the distinctive raised, bump-like structures that dot its surface like tiny blisters on tree bark. These warty protrusions are actually the lichen's reproductive structures, called perithecia, which push up through the crusty body creating the characteristic bumpy texture that makes this species so recognizable.
description: Branch Bumps is a crusty lichen that forms patches on tree bark, looking like someone splattered gray-white paint that dried into a bumpy, warty surface. The lichen body appears as irregular patches that can spread several inches across the bark, with a thick, crusty texture dotted with raised bumps. Each patch typically measures 2-6 inches across, though multiple patches often merge together to cover larger areas of trunk or branch.

idTips.label: Warty bumps
idTips.description: The surface is covered with distinctive raised bumps that feel hard and crusty when touched, like tiny volcanoes erupting from the lichen's surface

idTips.label: Thick crust
idTips.description: The lichen body forms a thick, chalky-feeling crust that's firmly attached to bark and difficult to scrape off with a fingernail

idTips.label: Gray-white color
idTips.description: Overall appearance is pale gray to whitish, sometimes with a slightly greenish tint when moist, resembling dried concrete or plaster

idTips.label: Bark preference
idTips.description: Almost always found on tree bark rather than rocks, favoring smooth-barked trees where it can form extensive patches

idTips.label: Irregular edges
idTips.description: Patches have wavy, irregular borders that blend into the bark rather than forming distinct circular shapes

habitat: Branch Bumps grows on the bark of deciduous trees throughout New England's forests, particularly favoring trees with smoother bark like maples, birches, and aspens. You'll find it from sea level to moderate elevations, most commonly in mixed hardwood forests and along forest edges where trees receive some direct sunlight. It seems to prefer mature trees and is often found 3-8 feet up the trunk where bark stays relatively dry.

seasonality.spring: The lichen becomes more vibrant as moisture returns, with the gray-white patches appearing slightly greener. This is an excellent time to spot it as the warty bumps are most pronounced before summer heat.
seasonality.summer: During dry periods, the lichen appears more chalky white and crusty, with the characteristic bumps standing out sharply against the bark. The texture feels particularly hard and brittle to the touch.
seasonality.fall: Autumn rains rejuvenate the lichen, making it appear slightly more colorful and easier to spot against the bark of leafless or changing trees.
seasonality.winter: The lichen remains visible and identifiable year-round, often appearing stark white against dark wet bark, making it one of the easier lichens to spot in the dormant season.

funFact: Branch Bumps is actually two organisms living as one - a fungus and an algae in partnership - and those warty bumps contain millions of fungal spores that can only germinate if they happen to land next to the exact right species of algae to restart the partnership!
confusionNotes: Branch Bumps is most easily confused with other crusty lichens on bark, but the distinctive raised warty bumps set it apart from smoother species. Remember: if it looks like bark with chickenpox, you've probably found Branch Bumps. Smoother crusty lichens lack these characteristic raised reproductive structures.
contextualKnowledge: **Note: Identification confidence is moderate** - with only 5 recorded observations in New England, specific field characteristics for this region may vary from general descriptions. The Pertusaria genus is known for being challenging to identify without microscopic examination, so definitive identification may require expert consultation.
compareHints: Branch Bumps differs from its Pertusaria relatives primarily in its habitat preference for bark over rock and its particularly pronounced warty bumps. Rock Wart Lichen grows on stone surfaces rather than trees, while Macoun's Wart Lichen typically has smaller, less prominent bumps and different chemical reactions when tested. The raised, blister-like reproductive structures of Branch Bumps are generally more dramatic than those of its cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rock Wart Lichen differs from its cousin Branch Bumps by growing exclusively on rock rather than tree bark, and from other Pertusaria species by its particularly thick, substantial crust and prominent warty structures.
Macoun's Wart Lichen differs from its Pertusaria relatives by having more prominent, well-defined warty bumps compared to the flatter Rock Wart Lichen or the more pustule-like Branch Bumps.
Unlike its more common relatives Rock Wart Lichen and Branch Bumps, this species shows distinctive reddish coloration rather than plain gray or white.
Unlike Rock Wart Lichen which forms obvious rounded bumps, or Branch Bumps which creates pustule-like growths, Pertusaria sulcata is distinguished by its grooved, furrowed surface texture.

Texas Wart Lichen differs from its Pertusaria relatives by having more distinctly rounded, wart-like bumps compared to the irregular lumps of Rock Wart Lichen or the pustule-like swellings of Branch Bumps.
